verified-feline-pleural-effusion-fip.findings: Source annotation describes dependent thoracic fluid, loss of visible cardiac margins and compressed/limited aerated lung.

verified-feline-pleural-effusion-fip.next: If dyspneic, stabilize first and consider oxygen and ultrasound-guided thoracocentesis where indicated; evaluate effusion and underlying cause.

exam2-case1-dsh.title: Exam 2 · Abdomen Cases · Abdomen case 1 · effusion, mixed intestinal gas and mass effect
exam2-case1-dsh.history: 10-year-old DSH cat. Anorexia; no other information provided.
exam2-case1-dsh.lookFor:
Describe serosal detail before choosing the most defensible differentials.
Work systematically: views and positioning, then each organ system (liver, spleen, stomach, small intestine, colon, kidneys, bladder), serosal and retroperitoneal detail, then Roentgen signs before naming a diagnosis.
exam2-case1-dsh.findings: Professor's notes: two views. Loss of serosal detail in the abdomen with a fluid-filled appearance (ascites). Increased radiolucency in the stomach, small intestine and colon; small-intestinal gas distension with multiple populations; greater gas distension in the fundus. Mass effect with leftward displacement. Small mineral/radiopaque material that appears to be bone in the intestines; some fecal material in the rectum and colon. If there were a perforation you would also expect free gas.
exam2-case1-dsh.interpretation: Differentials discussed in class: ruptured mass (neoplasia), hemoabdomen, foreign-body perforation, ascites (e.g., right-sided heart failure), distended bladder. Radiographs alone do not give the final diagnosis.

exam2-case3-dmh-hairties.findings: Professor's notes: abnormal arrangement of the small intestine ("tortuous turns", "stacking"). Mixed populations of intestinal diameter. Colon enlarged with fecal material (constipation). The border of the spleen is not clearly seen.
exam2-case3-dmh-hairties.interpretation: Equivocal. Rule-outs: constipation, foreign body, and ileus (functional or mechanical); the radiologist stated either. Plan discussed in class: enema, then repeat radiographs (the enema will introduce some gas). Decide on surgery from the clinical signs (GI signs, litter box); if the cat has not defecated within 1–2 hours, exploratory surgery is better than not, but be transparent with the owner about cost.
